turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning. Come through, the doctor's free. I took your observations a moment ago.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. What were the numbers?

[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Pulse a hundred and eight, blood pressure one twenty-two over seventy-six, oxygen ninety-nine percent, respiratory rate sixteen. A bit flushed, otherwise fine. Their partner is in the waiting room and said they'd wait.
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. I have been getting palpitations, and I become rather breathless with them. I thought it best to have it assessed properly.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Morning. Have a seat. Is it racing, skipped beats, or both?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Both, I think. It thumps in the centre of my chest, and then it seems to miss a beat.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is the breathlessness only with that, or does walking bring it on as well?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): Only with the palpitations. I can walk to the station with no difficulty at all.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has all this been going on?
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, last winter, or it might have been the winter before. I really cannot date it. I do apologise for being vague.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not at all. How often does it happen, and what makes it worse?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Most evenings, though not every day. It is worse at night, when I am trying to sleep, and worse again before an exam or a work meeting.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the work and the exams.

[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): I am a trainee accountant. I sit the professional papers, and I am in the office three days a week. My partner, who is waiting outside, says I sit bolt upright in bed and look pale and breathless, though I cannot vouch for the pale part.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with these spells?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): No. There is no chest pain. I would not describe it as pain.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you blacked out, or felt you might faint?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): I have not fainted. I do feel a little light-headed with the palpitations, but if I sit quietly it passes in a few minutes, and the thumping eases as well.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or swelling of the ankles? Do you wake gasping when the heart is not already racing?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): No cough, and my ankles are quite normal. I do not wake gasping unless the palpitations have already started.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): The way it clusters before exams, I wonder if stress is—
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I would not call it stress, Doctor. I am simply rather busy. I do not feel anxious as such, and I do not think this is psychological.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Understood. I am not calling it anxiety. I am only noting the timing. How much coffee do you drink?

[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): Four cups a day. Well, actually, it is nearer six, plus an energy drink most afternoons, two if a meeting runs late. I tried to cut down around Easter, but it did not stick.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): So six coffees and the energy drinks, still going. Do you smoke?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): I do not smoke cigarettes. I do vape, and I have done for about two years, rather more in the evenings when I am revising.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about alcohol?

[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Very little. A glass of wine at the weekend, if that. I share a flat with my partner and we hardly drink at home. The trains were dreadful this morning, which rather flustered me, though that is beside the point.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): The trains will do that to anyone. Any medicines you take yourself, prescribed or that you buy?

[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Nothing of my own. My sister takes biotin, the high-strength capsules, for her hair, and she suggested I try them, but I have not. My partner takes propranolol for migraines and offered me a tablet during an episode, which I declined.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Quite right not to take their propranolol. Any family history of heart disease, or thyroid trouble?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): My mother has an underactive thyroid, and she takes levothyroxine. There is no heart disease in the family, as far as I know.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): And for you, any medical conditions, or any operations?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): I have always been well. I have had no operations. I have never had a heart problem before these palpitations.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): None that I am aware of.

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me have a listen. Heart sounds are normal, the rhythm is regular just now, and there is no murmur. The chest is clear. Your pulse sitting here is still quick, about a hundred a minute.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Is a pulse of about a hundred a concern? I feel quite calm at this moment, oddly enough.

[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): I am thinking it through out loud. You are young, the caffeine intake is heavy, there is nicotine from the vape, and the spells come at night and before exams, yet the rhythm now is regular and the lungs are clear. My working impression is palpitations, most likely ectopic beats or a sinus tachycardia, driven by the coffee, the energy drinks and the vaping.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): So you do think the exams play a part, even though I do not feel stressed?

[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): The timing suggests a trigger, yes, without it amounting to anxiety. I still cannot rule out an overactive thyroid, especially with your mother's history, or an abnormal rhythm that is simply not happening while you sit here. Those remain possible until the results are back.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): What would you like to arrange?

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): An ECG, and thyroid bloods, that is a TSH and a free T4. I will have both done, so we can see whether this is the stimulants or whether the thyroid or the rhythm needs a closer look.
[SEG0044] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry to squeeze in. I can book the ECG for this afternoon in the treatment room, and you can take the blood form along to phlebotomy afterwards.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): This afternoon is perfectly convenient. Thank you.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): In the meantime, cut the coffee right down and stop the energy drinks for a fortnight, and ease off the vaping in the evenings if you can.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): I shall stop the energy drinks straight away. The coffee will take more discipline, but I will try.

[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): When a spell starts, breathe in for a count of four and out for a count of six, and stay sitting until the light-headed feeling has gone. That often settles this sort of thump.
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): In for four, out for six. I shall practise that.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you get chest pain, if you faint, or if the breathlessness stays on while you are resting and does not ease, go to A&E. Do not wait for me.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, of course. I understand.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): I will see you in a fortnight with the results, whether or not you are feeling better. If the ECG needs a quicker look, the staff will telephone you before then.
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): Might I bring my partner next time? They see the night-time episodes more clearly than I can.
[SEG0054] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Of course, that's fine. Come along with me and I'll fix the ECG time and the blood form.

spec.situation: Young adult with palpitations and breathlessness, worse at night and before exams or work meetings; downplays stress, drinks a lot of coffee and energy drinks, vapes; friend or partner contributes. Doctor orders ECG and thyroid tests, discusses breathing exercises.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

omissions.text: Palpitations are described as both a racing heartbeat and missed/skipped beats, with a thumping sensation in the centre of the chest.
Breathlessness occurs only with the palpitations; the patient can walk to the station without difficulty.
Partner reports the patient sometimes sits bolt upright in bed and looks pale and breathless during night-time episodes; patient cannot confirm the pallor.
Light-headedness passes in a few minutes and the thumping also eases if the patient sits quietly.
The patient is taking no prescribed or over-the-counter medicines of their own.
The energy drink intake can be two in an afternoon if a meeting runs late, not just one most afternoons.
Doctor explicitly stated they are not calling this anxiety, only noting the timing around exams/work meetings; there was some disagreement from the patient about stress/psychological attribution.
Family history wording was thyroid trouble in the family question, and the doctor specifically considered overactive thyroid despite the mother having underactive thyroid.
There is no medicine allergy or other allergy known ('None that I am aware of'), rather than a generic allergies negative without that wording.
ECG was booked for this afternoon in the treatment room, and the patient was to take the blood form to phlebotomy afterwards.
Follow-up was specified as in a fortnight whether or not the patient is feeling better.
Patient asked to bring their partner to the next appointment because the partner observes the night-time episodes more clearly; staff agreed this was fine.
